content_voiceover: This table is classic image-recognition material for boards — you need to match RBC shape to disease at a glance. Spherocytes are spheric with no central pallor and look microcytic; think hereditary spherocytosis or immune hemolytic anemia. Elliptocytes are oval, seen in hereditary elliptocytosis and megaloblastic anemia. Stomatocytes have a slit-like rather than round central pallor, classically from alcoholism or chronic liver disease, and also hereditary stomatocytosis. Acanthocytes, or spur cells, have five to ten irregular spicules of variable length and spacing — associate these with liver disease and abetalipoproteinemia. Echinocytes, or burr cells, have ten to thirty small, evenly spaced spicules, seen in uremia, pyruvate kinase deficiency, or as an artifact. Sickle cells are diagnostic of HbSS or HbSC disease. Target cells have a bullseye of central density and appear in thalassemia, hemoglobin C disorders, iron deficiency, liver disease, post-splenectomy, and LCAT deficiency. Schistocytes are the fragmented, helmet-shaped small cells of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, turbulent flow states like mechanical valves, and hemolytic uremic syndrome — always check a smear for schistocytes when you suspect TTP or HUS or DIC. The key exam trap is distinguishing spur cells, irregular and fewer, from burr cells, regular and numerous — spur cells mean liver disease, burr cells mean uremia or artifact.
keypoints: Spherocyte: no central pallor → HS, AIHA
Acanthocyte/spur cell (irregular spicules) → liver dz, abetalipoproteinemia
Echinocyte/burr cell (regular spicules) → uremia, PK deficiency, artifact
Target cell → thalassemia, liver dz, post-splenectomy
keypoint_voiceover: Key points for RBC morphology. Spherocytes lack central pallor and point to hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The classic exam trap is spur cells versus burr cells — spur cells have irregular, variable spicules and mean liver disease or abetalipoproteinemia, while burr cells have regular, numerous spicules and mean uremia, pyruvate kinase deficiency, or artifact. Target cells suggest thalassemia, liver disease, or post-splenectomy state. Schistocytes are the hallmark of microangiopathic hemolysis, so think TTP, HUS, DIC, or a mechanical valve.
